expansion:
Cataract is the keyed answer because blunt trauma is a recognised direct cause of an acute lens opacity, and the lecture names this exact picture: “SLIDE 32/33 — Blunt trauma: Rosette-shaped cataract” with a red-reflex photograph illustrating it (L25, slide 32/33). A stick injury to the globe is blunt trauma, and a rosette-shaped (posterior subcapsular, star-shaped) cataract forming over the following weeks to months after such an injury is a well-described post-traumatic lens change, which fits a white pupil appearing two months after the stick injury in a child whose vision was normal beforehand.

Retinoblastoma, option B, is excluded by the history rather than by absence of leukocoria as a feature: the lecture on leukocoria differentials lists retinoblastoma as the "most dangerous" cause of a white pupil in a child (L33,34, page 18), but retinoblastoma is an intraocular tumour that is already present and growing before any trauma, so it would not explain a previously and repeatedly documented normal eye that only turns white after a discrete traumatic event two months earlier. The temporal link to trauma with a prior normal record argues against a pre-existing tumour and for an acquired traumatic cataract instead.

Retinopathy of prematurity, option C, is a disease of preterm, low-birth-weight infants with abnormal retinal vascularisation, and the lecture's own leukocoria list ties it to prematurity, not to an otherwise normal 6-year-old with a clear traumatic precipitant (L33,34, page 18); nothing in the vignette suggests prematurity, and ROP would already have been apparent in earlier normal examinations, which the history rules out.

Corneal degeneration, option D, would produce an anterior corneal opacity rather than a true retro-pupillary leukocoria; the lecture's leukocoria differential is built entirely around lens- and retina-level causes (congenital cataract, retinoblastoma, ROP, Coats disease, PFV, Toxoplasma, Toxocara, retinal dysplasia) and does not include corneal degeneration among them (L33,34, page 18), and it also has no established link to acute trauma in a previously normal eye (not taken from the course material).
objective: Recognise post-traumatic (blunt) cataract as a cause of delayed leukocoria in a child with a prior normal eye examination
